name: default
note: Rules chosen for confidence rather than coverage. A rule that fires on a busy but healthy host teaches the analyst to ignore its whole category, so a signal earns a place here only when it is rare in normal operation or is qualified by a second, independent one. Dump actions are recommended only where the evidence is strong enough to justify writing live malicious code to the examiner's workstation: the two critical injection rules, hollowing, ghosting, and a PE image in a .NET process's private memory (in the last two, memory is the only copy). PROC-INJECT is deliberately excluded — a bare malfind region is why that rule is only medium, and suggesting a dump for each one would undo the distinction. Dumps are never executed unless --dump is given; the analyst is handed the command instead.

rules.title: Injected process has external network activity
rules.note: A malfind region alone is common enough to be noise. The same region in a process talking to a routable address is the shape of a live implant.

rules.title: Suspicious thread executing in unbacked memory
rules.note: A thread whose start address lies outside any mapped module, in a process that also has executable private memory, is code that was written and then run.

rules.title: PE image in the executable private memory of a .NET process
rules.note: A .NET process trips malfind by design: its JIT compiles into executable private memory, which is why PROC-INJECT annotates such a process rather than escalating it. What the JIT never produces is a PE header. A region beginning with MZ in a process that hosts the runtime is a whole image placed in memory without a file behind it — the shape of Assembly.Load(byte[]) tradecraft and of a DLL reflectively injected into a .NET host — and is the case the annotation must not be allowed to explain away. High rather than critical because legitimate software does embed assemblies as resources and load them from memory; the dump is suggested because the image on disk, if there is one, is not this one. Scoped to .NET processes deliberately: that is where malfind is otherwise expected, so that is where the discriminator earns its keep. malfind_mz is a signal in its own right, so a pack may widen this to every process by dropping the dotnet_runtime clause.

rules.title: Running process absent from the active process list
rules.note: Recovered by pool scan, missing from the linked list, and carrying no exit time. The exit-time clause is what separates this from every process that has simply terminated.

rules.title: Possible process hollowing
rules.note: The mapped image does not match the file it claims to come from.

rules.title: Possible process ghosting
rules.note: The image file was marked for deletion before the section was mapped, so there is no file on disk to examine. The memory is the only copy — which is why this rule suggests a dump even though it is only high.

rules.title: Process visible to one enumeration method but not another
rules.note: Cross-view discrepancy reported by PsXView. Kept alongside PROC-HIDDEN deliberately: the two derive the same conclusion by different routes, and disagreement between them is itself worth reading.

rules.title: Several independent anomalies on one process
rules.note: No single signal here is conclusive. Three at once on the same process is not a coincidence worth explaining away.

rules.title: System binary running from the wrong directory
rules.note: A process carrying the name of a fixed Windows binary whose image is not where Windows keeps it. Judged on the kernel's own record of the image path, not the PEB, which the process can rewrite. Parent and name can both be correct here — this asks the separate question of what is actually executing.

rules.title: Service-only process running in an interactive session
rules.note: svchost, services, lsass and wininit belong to session 0. csrss and winlogon are excluded from the check because one of each exists per session.

rules.title: System process running as an unexpected account
rules.note: lsass, services and wininit run as SYSTEM. svchost is excluded: LocalService and NetworkService are legitimate for it.

rules.title: Process launched through an execution proxy, with a suspicious command line
rules.note: The parent is a binary whose purpose in a chain is to hide the real launcher, and the command line independently looks like tradecraft. Either alone is worth a look; together they are the shape of a pasted or scripted intrusion.

rules.title: Process launched through an execution proxy
rules.note: Parent is pcalua, WmiPrvSE, mshta or forfiles — each a documented way to break the parent/child relationship an examiner would otherwise follow. Deliberately not ancestry-based: the chain above a proxy is precisely what it falsifies.

rules.title: Office-spawned shell with external network activity
rules.note: A document application has no reason to produce a command interpreter, and one that then talks to a routable address is the standard opening move of a macro or ClickFix delivery.

rules.title: Office application spawned a command interpreter
rules.note: Derived from ancestry rather than the immediate parent, so a loader placed between the document and the shell does not conceal the relationship.

rules.title: Browser spawned a command interpreter
rules.note: Browsers spawn helpers and updaters constantly, but not cmd or PowerShell. Ancestry-based, for the same reason as the Office rule.

rules.title: Encoded command line with external network activity
rules.note: A base64 payload passed to -EncodedCommand is a deliberate attempt to keep the command out of logs. Paired with a routable connection it is not administration.

rules.title: Base64-encoded command line
rules.note: Legitimate tooling does use -EncodedCommand to avoid quoting problems, which is why this is not critical on its own.

rules.title: Script engine spawned a signed execution proxy
rules.note: wscript, cscript or mshta launching regsvr32, rundll32, certutil or similar. The signed binary is what runs the payload, which is the point of the technique.

rules.title: Command line matching a known execution technique
rules.note: Kept at medium on its own: administrators do write scripts that download and invoke code. The rules above escalate it when something independent agrees.

rules.title: Executable memory not backed by a file
rules.note: Malfind on its own. Every JIT compiler on the host produces this, so it is listed for completeness rather than escalated. The higher-severity rules above are the ones that qualify it. The evidence line says whether the process hosts the .NET runtime and whether any region begins with an MZ header, so a hit on a .NET process reads as what it is without being reasoned out afresh each time — and without being suppressed: the finding still stands, annotated. The one .NET case that is not the JIT, an MZ-headed region, is excluded here because PROC-DOTNET-MZ raises it.

rules.title: System-call table entry points outside the kernel
rules.note: Nothing but ntoskrnl and win32k has any business owning an SSDT entry. Patch-guard makes this rare on modern x64, which is exactly why a hit matters.

rules.title: Kernel module recovered by scan but absent from the loaded list
rules.note: The kernel analogue of a hidden process. Unlike a process there is no exit time to guard against: an unloaded driver's entry is removed outright, so a scan hit with no list entry is a live discrepancy.

rules.title: Driver object whose start address matches no known module
rules.note: Registering a driver from a hidden module is a standard rootkit technique. DriverModule reports only the disconnects, so a row is already the anomaly; the known-exception clause drops the ones upstream has confirmed benign.

rules.title: Kernel callback owned by no identifiable module
rules.note: A notification callback that resolves to no loaded module is code the kernel calls and the module list does not admit to.

rules.title: Service hosted by a process with injected code
rules.note: A service is only as trustworthy as the process running it. This is the correlation the service entity exists for: it carries the finding from the process back to the persistence mechanism that will restart it.

rules.title: Service hidden from the service manager's own list
rules.note: SvcDiff yields only the difference between scanning for service records and walking the manager's list, so every row it produces is already the anomaly — presence is the whole condition. Note it runs only on Windows 10 15063+ 64-bit; on older images it yields nothing, which reads the same here as finding nothing.

rules.title: Service binary in a user-writable directory
rules.note: Services run as SYSTEM and start on boot; a binary under Users, Temp or AppData is a persistence pattern rather than a deployment one. ProgramData is deliberately excluded — legitimate updaters use it often enough to drown the signal.
